APATITE

When a young rock collector asks, “Have you lost

your apatite?” he is not asking about your interest in

food but is speaking about the mineral by that name. He

is probably making a joke of its name. The name really

means “to deceive” for it is very easily mistaken for

other minerals.

The phosphate group is a very large one, and apatite

is the only one that can be considered a common min-

eral. Apatite is véry widely distributed. Grains and small

crystals are found in rocks of all kinds, and it occurs in

sedimentary beds.

Vi

In eastern Canada, large amounts of apatite are mined

for use in making baking powder, also for making phos-

phate, an important plant food or fertilizer.

Apatite is of special interest to rock collectors because

=

of its very beautiful, transparent, colorful and distinctive

crystals. Large crystals are rather rare. They can be

found in pegmatites. Beautifully cut gems are displayed in

museum cases, but apatite crystals are too soft to be

worn as jewelry (they can be cut with a knife). Rare
